transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-05
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 min
Attendees: Lina (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Aisha (Product), Evan (Verdant Eng Lead), Priya (Verdant ML Platform), Sam (CTO)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/KV cache recommendations for Verdant's multi-turn support agent use case. Covered trade-offs between latency and unit cost, a 3-scenario cost model (baseline, optimized batching, optimized batching + prefix cache), and next steps to run a small pilot with Verdant traffic.

Topics covered:
- Current Verdant workload characteristics and SLAs
- Batching strategies (continuous batching vs fixed intervals)
- Prefix (KV) cache for repeated system+user prefixes across conversations
- Cost model assumptions and example math (tokens saved, throughput improvements)
- Deployment modes: Hosted vs Dedicated implications for batching
- Fallbacks and correctness tradeoffs when using cache and quantized model variants

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Lina: ok everyone i think we're recording, thanks for making time. quick intros?
[00:00:08] Evan: evan here, engineering lead at verdant, we own the chat infra for support assistant.
[00:00:12] Priya: priya, ml platform, looking to reduce token spend and keep latency sub-300ms p95 for simple prompts.
[00:00:18] Sam: sam, cto, interested in economics — basically can we cut costs without breaking sla.
[00:00:23] Marcus: marcus, inference se at redwood, i'll lead the batching/cache portions and run the numbers.
[00:00:27] Lina: great. quick context: verdant sends about 14 QPS at peak per tenant, average 3-turn conversations, common system prompt + user history reuse on 60% of sessions. does that match what you shared?
[00:00:40] Priya: yeah that's the ballpark — we see a long tail of prompts but a lot of repeated templates.
[00:00:45] Marcus: perfect. i'll first sketch the cost model then demo the optimize console where we can simulate hit rates and batching profiles.

[00:01:12] Marcus: so baseline: one request = full context run, no cache. assume average 500 prompt tokens (incl. system + history) and 150 response tokens, we charge per output+input token — in our model cost per 1k tokens is X but i'll show relative savings. Baseline token count ~650 tokens per call. at 14 qps peak that's ~9.1k tokens/sec.
[00:01:45] Evan: hold on, our metrics show many calls start with the same 80-token system prompt, and then the variable user prompt. is that what you mean by reuse?
[00:01:51] Marcus: exactly — that 80-token prefix is a candidate for prefix cache. if we cache transformed KV state after the prefix, subsequent calls only compute from the suffix.

[00:02:18] [00:02:18] Marcus: demoing Optimize console --> (screen share noises) you can see a cost simulator: you can toggle batching latency targets, max batch size, and prefix cache hit rate. i set three scenarios:
- Scenario A (baseline): no cache, minimal batching (1-3ms scheduling), mean latency 220ms, cost baseline 100%
- Scenario B (batching tuned): batching window 20ms, continuous batching, throughput up ~1.6x, mean latency 260ms, cost ~65% of baseline
- Scenario C (batching + prefix cache 60% hit): same batching + prefix cache -> effective tokens processed drop ~40%, cost ~40% of baseline, p95 latency holds at ~300ms with cache warm paths

[00:04:10] Priya: those percentages are helpful — can you show the math for the 40% tokens reduction?
[00:04:16] Marcus: yes. quick math on a representative minute: 14 qps * 60 = 840 calls. Baseline tokens = 840 * 650 = 546k tokens. With prefix cache at 60% hit, for 60% of calls we skip the 80-token prefix processing and KV ops only add ~10 tokens overhead for replay, so effective tokens per hit call = 650 - 70 = 580. that saves 70 tokens per hit -> 840 * 0.6 * 70 = 35,280 tokens saved in a minute. plus batching reduces per-call overhead and improves throughput allowing smaller per-token GPU amortization which we represent as a 35% cost reduction from batching alone. compose those effects leads to ~60% reduction vs baseline? oh i need to be careful, i should show combined product, we had earlier ~40% total.
[00:05:12] Evan: i noticed some rounding there. can you export the exact spreadsheet?
[00:05:16] Marcus: yes i'll export the Optimize simulation CSV after the call.

[00:05:40] Aisha: quick product note — we recommend measuring warm-cache vs cold-cache p95 because first request for a prefix still pays full cost, and cache TTL matters.
[00:05:50] Priya: what's the recommended TTL? our users have long-lived conversations sometimes.
[00:05:54] Marcus: TTL depends. common pattern: keep prefix cache in-memory for 5-30 minutes for session reuse. if conversations are long, session-level caching + streaming kv updates works. for compliance, you can pin prefixes to private deployments to keep them in-customer memory.

[00:06:30] [00:06:30] Marcus: demo continues - show continuous batching knobs: batching window (ms), max batch size, concurrency targets. trade-offs: larger window = higher batch sizes = better throughput & lower unit cost, but increases tail latency. we plotted p50/p95/p99 as window changes. at 20ms window p95 ~260ms; at 100ms window p95 ~450ms.
[00:07:10] Sam: is 20ms realistic for our infra? we're on k8s nodes with autoscaler and a mix of small GPUs.
[00:07:16] Marcus: yes if you use Dedicated pools with pinned gpus and conservative concurrency you can do 10-30ms windows. Hosted also supports similar, but under noisy multi-tenant loads Dedicated gives tighter SLOs.

[00:07:50] Evan: what about quantization? i heard quantized models are cheaper but sometimes slower at long sequences.
[00:07:56] Marcus: correct, 4-bit quantization reduces memory and inference cost. for shorter outputs quantized models can be slightly faster, for very long sequences the kernel behavior matters. our cost model includes a quantization delta factor; we'll include both quantized and fp16 scenarios in the export.

[00:08:30] [00:08:30] Marcus: now a rough dedicated vs hosted cost note: for sustained 14 qps with predictable traffic, Dedicated with reserved pools reduces token unit cost by ~25-40% relative to Hosted for same model family because of amortized infra. but Dedicated adds base monthly capacity costs. we'll put exact numbers per scenario.

[00:09:10] Priya: ok let's talk failure modes: when prefix cache returns stale state could that change model outputs?
[00:09:18] Marcus: possibility yes — if your system prompt changes, you need cache invalidation. best practice: include prefix version hash in cache key and invalidate on rollouts. also add canary route that bypasses cache during model rollouts.

[00:09:42] Evan: how do you handle prefix cache with multi-tenant isolation?
[00:09:47] Marcus: cache keys include tenant id and optional VPC scoping. in Redwood Private/Dedicated you can opt to keep cache in-customer VPC to meet compliance.

[00:10:05] [00:10:05] Marcus: i'm going to run a short simulated load with your rough distribution (i'll use a synthetic trace with 14 qps peak, 3-turn convs, 60% prefix reuse). (sound of typing) starting sim...
[00:11:00] Marcus: results in the console: baseline cost per hour vs optimized scenarios. baseline $xx/hr (we obfuscated full numbers on-screen but i'll put them in the export). optimize scenario 1 (batching) $0.65x and scenario 2 (batching + prefix cache) ~$0.42x baseline.
[00:11:30] Priya: can you break that down to tokens saved vs infra amortization?
[00:11:36] Marcus: yes two buckets: direct token savings from cache and efficiency gains from batching which reduce per-token GPU overhead. i showed a chart: direct token savings ~15% from 60% prefix hits (because we don't eliminate whole prefix in all cases due to overhead), batching effect roughly 35% improvement in unit economics. combined multiplicative effect ~0.55 * 0.65 = 0.36 (i may have slight rounding) -> roughly 36% of baseline cost.

[00:12:30] Evan: these multipliers are quite optimistic, what if our real-world hit rate is 30% not 60%?
[00:12:36] Marcus: good question — i toggled to 30% hit in the console: combined effect drops to ~0.55*0.8 ~= 0.44 of baseline. so still material but less dramatic. we'll include a sensitivity table in the CSV export.

[00:13:10] Aisha: note for the team — Optimize can auto-suggest batching window given desired p95 and cost target; it's not magic but a heuristic based on your latency envelope and sequence length distribution.

[00:13:45] [00:13:45] Marcus: switching to edge cases: multi-turn where user history differs slightly we can still use partial prefix caching (store the KV state after common system + first user message), then replay subsequent deltas — that reduces effective tokens but increases complexity.
[00:14:20] Priya: how do we estimate engineering effort? we're worried about integrating cache keys + invalidation into our existing session store.
[00:14:28] Marcus: typical integration is 2-3 sprint tasks: identify canonical prefixes, implement keying in session service, add cache TTL + invalidation hooks. we can provide a starter repo and a migration checklist.

[00:15:00] Evan: about correctness: do you see any hallucination risk from skipping recomputation of prefix state?
[00:15:06] Marcus: not usually — prefix cache stores KV cache (internal attention tensors) rather than textual shortcuts; it's equivalent to having already run the prefix. correctness is maintained so long as prefix and model version match. major risk is stale cache after prompt template changes.

[00:15:40] Sam: what's the recommended rollout plan?
[00:15:44] Marcus: canary at 5% traffic with disabled cache to compare outputs, then 25%, monitoring quality metrics (answer correctness, latency, some fuzzy match evals). Redwood has A/B rollout tooling for that.

[00:16:10] Priya: let's talk monitoring — how do we detect cache-induced regressions?
[00:16:15] Marcus: track per-route quality metrics, synthetic prompts (promptset evals) and a sample of live responses compared against baseline; set alerts for deviations beyond threshold. Redwood Optimize ties eval regressions to deployments.

[00:16:52] [00:16:52] Marcus: i'll highlight one more Optimize feature: prefix hit curve simulation. you can upload a small trace and it'll estimate hit rate for different keying strategies (strict template match vs fuzzy key). that dramatically changes predicted savings. please share your 7-day sample and we'll run it.

[00:17:30] Evan: ok we'll pull that and send. question on billing — how is token accounting with KV cache represented on invoices?
[00:17:37] Marcus: invoices reflect actual tokens processed by model runtime. cache-hit requests that skip token decoding still incur small KV overhead tokens (we model as a small fixed token cost) — the invoice shows breakdown of input tokens, output tokens, and infra surcharge.

[00:18:05] Priya: curious about worst-case cold start + cache miss tails — any guidance to keep p99 under control?
[00:18:12] Marcus: use a hybrid: short TTL + pre-warm common prefixes, keep a small standby pool or burst capacity (Dedicated burst), and set fallback policy to a smaller low-latency model during spikes.

[00:18:45] [00:18:45] Marcus: technical sidebar: KV cache stores kv key/value layers; we persist them in redis-like stores for Private deployments or in local memory for Hosted. private option allows you to store them in your VPC.

[00:19:20] Evan: are there security concerns with storing KV cache? tokens might contain PII.
[00:19:24] Marcus: yes store them with encryption at rest and in transit. Redwood Private gives you customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and audit logs. we also support redaction on cache keys.

[00:19:50] Priya: question from infra: how does batch packing handle mixed sequence lengths?
[00:19:56] Marcus: our runtime does dynamic batching and sequence bucketing; small extra padding costs exist but we optimize kernel selection to minimize per-token compute. Optimize will show distribution bucketed efficiency.

[00:20:30] Sam: do you have a recommended set of thresholds for us to start with? latency goal 300ms p95 and keep cost below 50% of baseline.
[00:20:36] Marcus: start with 20ms batching window, max batch size tuned to your GPU (we'll estimate), prefix cache TTL 10 minutes, and conservative cache keying (tenant+template+version). Monitor quality and bump cache aggressiveness if quality stays stable.

[00:21:10] [00:21:10] Marcus: now i want to walk through a short demo of a particular conversation flow and show prefix cache hit/miss traces in the console logs. (console noises) here's a session where first call populates cache, second call hits it and saves ~65 tokens, you can see latency drop by ~25ms on the warm path.

[00:22:05] Priya: those logs look great. can we stream similar telemetry into datadog?
[00:22:10] Marcus: yes consoles supports forwarders to datadog and prometheus metrics for hits, misses, avg saved tokens. we can share the schema.

[00:22:40] Evan: you mentioned fallback model variants earlier — can you expand on policy?
[00:22:46] Marcus: policy example: if queue depth > threshold or latency spike, route to a small quantized model with lower cost; also have region fallback or lower tier capacity. Redwood routing layer lets you set rule priorities.

[00:23:20] [00:23:20] Lina: moving toward wrap-up — what do you want from Verdant to run the next pilot?
[00:23:25] Priya: we'll send the 7-day trace plus a list of 5 canonical prompts and indicate which templates we expect to reuse.
[00:23:32] Sam: and i'll need a rough cost delta to present to CFO — show hosted vs dedicated with steady-state numbers.

[00:23:40] Marcus: noted — i'll include hosted vs dedicated amortized scenarios and show break-even month given your traffic.

[00:24:05] [00:24:05] Marcus: quick Q&A volley:
[00:24:10] Evan: do you support server-side prompt rewriting before cache keying?
[00:24:14] Marcus: yes you can normalize templates before keying; Optimize supports pluggable normalizers in simulation.
[00:24:22] Priya: what about concurrency limits per tenant?
[00:24:26] Marcus: per-tenant concurrency and rate limiters are supported; autoscale policies are per customer in Dedicated.

[00:24:45] Aisha: i'll follow-up with the migration checklist, sample repo and a short runbook for prefix keying patterns.
[00:24:52] Lina: perfect. final recap?

[00:25:00] Recap (live):
- Redwood will send CSV export with three scenarios (baseline, batching tuned, batching + prefix cache) and sensitivity table for hit rates and batch windows.
- Verdant will provide sample trace + canonical prompts.
- SE-led benchmark scheduled week of 2025-11-17.

[00:25:30] Closing chatter and minor crosstalk, then small side discussion about potential POC timeline and procurement notes.

[00:26:10] (Call recording continues with a 26 minute technical deep dive between Marcus and Priya: they talk specifics about redis cluster sizing, eviction policies for cache TTL, and a pseudo-config for the session service.)

[00:26:15] Marcus: for redis sizing, assume average cache entry ~3KB (kv tensors serialized compressed), with 60% hit rates estimated at 840 calls/minute, you might need a few GB of memory per tenant for warm caches, but in Dedicated we co-locate and partition.
[00:27:00] Priya: hm 3KB seems high, we're concerned about memory costs.
[00:27:05] Marcus: it's conservative — we can compress and prune. also we can store only top-N hot prefixes.

[00:28:00] [00:28:00] (They map out eviction policy and show a sample redis ttl config and LRU thresholds, some transcription mistakes here: "LRU thrshold" spelled odd.)

[00:33:00] (Later Marcus demos a small script that replays trace to optimize cache keying; he shows a ~10% improvement after switching from naive keying to template-based keying.)
